out: The Palestinian Authority officially joined the International Criminal Court (ICC) as its 123rd member, granting the court jurisdiction over alleged crimes in Palestinian territories since June 2014. The move, celebrated by the Palestinians and human rights groups as a step toward justice and accountability, has been opposed by Israel and the United States, who argue Palestine is not a state and thus ineligible for membership. Despite objections, the ICC maintains that Palestine qualifies as a state under the Rome Statute and has already launched a preliminary examination into possible war crimes.

Now under the care of foster caregiver Sara Mellado, Theia is recovering from severe injuries like a dislocated jaw and sinus damage, with a fundraising campaign surpassing $10,000 to cover her medical expenses. Mohammad Javad Zarif, Iran's foreign minister and key negotiator in the nuclear deal with the U.S., is known for his diplomatic charm and polished demeanor, earning him a hero's welcome upon returning to Iran. Despite his prominent role, lesser-known facts reveal he was educated in the U.S., has a disputed birth year, and faced a U.S. federal investigation over his alleged ties to the Alavi Foundation. His public exchanges, including a notable Twitter exchange with a U.S. politician about Holocaust denial, highlight his complex and often surprising persona on the global stage.

They were healthcare workers for Partners in Health who had contact with a colleague who was diagnosed with Ebola and is now in fair condition at the National Institutes of Health. A Duke University student has admitted to hanging a noose made of rope near a student union, prompting a campus-wide response and ongoing criminal and student conduct investigations. The incident, which sparked protests and a large gathering at Duke Chapel, was condemned by university leaders as a "cowardly act," with President Richard Brodhead denouncing it as unrepresentative of the university's values. The event is part of a broader pattern of racially charged incidents on U.S. college campuses, including recent noose hangings and hate speech cases at other institutions.

The heartfelt prom-posal, complete with flowers, a Taylor Swift-themed poster, and approval from Ellie’s parents, was inspired by Trey’s involvement in a school program called Best Buddies, which fosters friendships between students with and without developmental disabilities. Both Ellie and her family are thrilled, and Trey plans to study special education in college, inspired by the experience.

Tropical storm Maysak, now known as Chedeng in the Philippines, is approaching the country with sustained winds over 70 mph and gusts up to 90 mph, prompting warnings of flash floods and landslides. Authorities have banned outdoor activities, evacuated some areas, and barred tourists from entering coastal regions like Aurora, while officials urge residents to prepare for a potentially severe impact. The storm is expected to make landfall Sunday morning on the southeastern coast of Isabela province and exit the Philippines by Monday.

For the first time in eight years, Bob Barker made a surprise return to "The Price Is Right," hosting the opening segment of the April 1 episode. At 91, the legendary host, who stepped down in 2007 after 35 years, appeared spry and in full form, handling the "Lucky Seven" game before handing over the reins to current host Drew Carey. The nostalgic moment delighted fans and marked a heartfelt tribute to Barker’s enduring legacy on the show.

A 19-year-old UK national from northwest London, Yahya Rashid, was arrested at Luton Airport upon his return from Turkey and charged with terror offenses. He faces two charges related to planning terrorist acts and assisting others in committing terrorism between November 1 and March 31. Rashid is scheduled to appear in Westminster Magistrates' Court.

New research by the Anne Frank House reveals that Anne and her sister Margot likely died in February 1945, not in March as previously believed, based on survivor testimonies and archival records. The sisters, who endured horrific conditions in Bergen-Belsen, were exposed to lice and overcrowding, which facilitated a deadly typhus outbreak, with symptoms appearing before February 7—making survival past that point unlikely. Despite their tragic deaths, Anne’s diary remains a powerful testament to hope and resilience.

Michele Bachmann sparked backlash by comparing President Obama to the co-pilot of the Germanwings flight, accusing him of recklessly endangering the U.S. through his Iran nuclear deal. Her inflammatory Facebook comment drew widespread criticism for being disrespectful and politically divisive, with many calling it inappropriate and attention-seeking. The comparison came amid tense negotiations over Iran’s nuclear program, with a June 30 deadline looming for a comprehensive agreement.

Louis Jordan, a 37-year-old fisherman, was rescued after drifting for 66 days in a capsized 35-foot sailboat, surviving by collecting rainwater, catching fish attracted to his laundry, and enduring multiple storms. He was found by the crew of the container ship *Houston Express* off the coast of Virginia, appearing in surprisingly good condition despite extreme hardships. Authorities have confirmed no reason to doubt his story, and his family expressed shock at his resilience and relatively stable health after such an ordeal.

The ongoing California drought, now in its fourth year, is having nationwide economic impacts, particularly on food prices, as California produces over a third of the nation’s vegetables and nearly two-thirds of its fruits and nuts. Prices for items like berries, broccoli, grapes, and packaged salad rose significantly in 2014 due to the drought, and while some prices have since dropped, experts warn that reduced crop planting and continued dry conditions could lead to higher grocery bills again this year. The FBI has charged Keonna Thomas, a 30-year-old Philadelphia woman, with attempting to travel overseas to fight for ISIS, citing her use of social media to express extremist views and her purchase of a visa to Turkey and a flight to Barcelona. She is one of three women arrested this week, including two in New York accused of planning to build explosive devices for attacks in the U.S. The Justice Department has seen a rise in cases involving support to terrorist groups, particularly ISIS, highlighting the growing threat posed by decentralized, internet-fueled radicalization.

Iran plans to lift its ban on women attending some men's sports events, starting within the next year, according to Deputy Sports Minister Abdolhamid Ahmadi, who said the change will initially apply to indoor sports. The move, which follows international pressure and protests, marks a potential shift from decades of exclusion, though women will still be barred from many events, particularly outdoor sports like soccer. The decision comes amid global scrutiny, including criticism from FIFA, and follows high-profile incidents such as female fans watching Iran’s team during the Asian Cup in Australia.

Online platforms have become vital outlets for dissent in authoritarian countries, offering a low-cost, accessible alternative to mainstream media, though governments often respond with legal pressure or arrests. In Singapore, bloggers like Amos Yee and Roy Ngerng face defamation charges and severe consequences for criticizing leaders, reflecting a broader pattern of using the courts to silence critics. Similar crackdowns occur in Malaysia and Vietnam, with China leading globally in imprisoning journalists and bloggers, particularly from ethnic minority groups.

Singer Avril Lavigne has revealed she was bedridden for five months due to undiagnosed Lyme disease, which she believes was contracted after a tick bite. She described severe symptoms including inability to move, breathe, or speak, and said the illness felt like she was dying, with her health deteriorating to the point where she couldn’t shower for days. Now 80% recovered, Lavigne is releasing a new single to support the 2015 Special Olympics and says her illness was a life-changing wake-up call that has renewed her appreciation for life.

Other Indian states like Haryana have also imposed strict penalties, and India’s Home Minister has pledged to push for a nationwide law against cow slaughter.

FBI agents and local law enforcement pursued 36-year-old Kevone Charleston, a suspect in 32 armed commercial robberies since 2013, after he attempted to rob a CVS in Forsyth County, Georgia. During the high-speed chase, Charleston rammed multiple government vehicles, injuring two FBI agents, and was eventually shot and captured 8 feet from the median. The FBI described the incident as the conclusion of a lengthy investigation, noting Charleston’s history of armed confrontations and the agents’ readiness for such a scenario.

A total lunar eclipse occurred on the morning of September 28, 2015, lasting just four minutes and 43 seconds—the shortest of the century—visible across much of North America, parts of South America, Asia, and Russia, with the best views in the western U.S. The moon turned a reddish hue, often called a "blood moon," due to Earth's atmosphere filtering out blue light. Al-Shabaab has claimed responsibility for a deadly attack on Garissa University College in Kenya, resulting in numerous deaths and hostages, marking a significant escalation in the group's ongoing campaign of violence across East Africa. The militant group, rooted in Somalia's civil war and aligned with al-Qaeda, has long targeted Kenya in retaliation for its military involvement in Somalia and to advance its radical Islamist agenda. The attack underscores a deepening regional crisis fueled by extremist ideology, cross-border conflict, and the complex interplay of local, national, and international factors.

Easter, a central Christian holiday celebrating Christ's resurrection, is determined by a complex calculation involving the lunar cycle and the vernal equinox, which is why its date shifts each year—coinciding this year with a blood moon. While Western Christians celebrate Easter on the first Sunday after the first full moon following the vernal equinox, Eastern Orthodox Christians use the Julian calendar, resulting in a different date, often a week later. The scandal involved thousands of athletes who were funneled into fake classes with falsified grades to maintain eligibility, undermining the NCAA’s own claims about academic integrity. Critics, including former officials and whistleblowers, accuse the NCAA of hypocrisy, saying its actions contradict its long-standing rhetoric about prioritizing education.

The juvenile court denied her release and visitation rights, rejecting arguments from her attorney and mother that she is mature enough to make her own medical decisions. Although doctors say she is doing well and her treatment is nearly complete, the Department of Children and Families continues to hold custody, citing concerns over her safety and the need to protect her from self-harm, despite her wishes to return home.

Antarctica may have recorded its highest temperature ever—63.5°F (15.5°C)—on March 24 at Argentina's Esperanza Base on the Antarctic Peninsula, according to Weather Underground and CNN. An international committee of top climatologists and meteorologists is now reviewing the measurement's accuracy, examining equipment, procedures, and nearby records, with a final determination expected by late summer or early fall. Scientists closely monitor such extreme weather events in Antarctica as key indicators of global climate change.

Chelsea Manning, an imprisoned soldier serving a 35-year sentence for leaking classified documents to WikiLeaks, has begun using Twitter through a voice phone and a third-party communications firm, Fitzgibbon Media, due to her lack of direct internet access. She identifies as transgender, having been granted legal recognition as Chelsea Elizabeth Manning and authorized for hormone therapy while incarcerated. Manning, who was convicted on 20 of 22 charges including espionage, has previously contributed opinion pieces to major publications from prison.

President Barack Obama's strong political investment in reaching a nuclear deal with Iran has driven the negotiations, creating perceptions that the U.S. is desperate for an agreement, despite Iran's economic struggles from sanctions. This political pressure has weakened America's negotiating position, emboldened Iran, and alarmed U.S. allies in the Middle East, sparking fears of a regional nuclear arms race and contributing to conflicts like the war in Yemen. While a solid deal would be desirable, the current framework appears compromised by political urgency rather than strategic clarity.

"Furious 7," the final film featuring the late Paul Walker, is on track for a massive $135 million–$138 million opening weekend in North America, fueled by global momentum and emotional resonance, with a record-breaking $60 million earned internationally in its first two days. The film, which opened in 4,003 U.S. theaters and over 10,500 screens worldwide, is poised to surpass previous April openings and become the largest domestic debut since 2013, aided by its unprecedented release scale and tribute to Walker.

The decision, welcomed by activists and officials alike, is seen as a hopeful beginning, though broader change will require national legislation to achieve full equality.

The discussion reflects a long-standing, if quirky, interest in extraterrestrial life within Japan's political and cultural landscape.

Kaminsky said he accepted the apology and was "over it," noting they had spoken and he felt no ill will. The incident occurred during a high-profile game that drew the largest Final Four audience in 22 years.

Sisters Iman and Siham Hashi, known as Faarrow, are a Somali-Canadian Afro-pop duo based in Los Angeles, where they are recording their debut album with producer Elijah Kelley. Iraq has deployed hundreds of additional troops, including federal police, a quick reaction force, and members of the Shia-led Hasd Al-Shaabi militia, to reinforce forces defending the strategically vital Baiji oil refinery from an ISIS assault. The attack, which began four days prior, saw ISIS claim control of parts of the refinery, though Iraqi officials maintained they still held full control. The refinery, located 40 kilometers from Tikrit, is critical to Iraq’s domestic fuel supply, and any damage could have major economic and strategic consequences.

Tokyo Electric Power Company (TEPCO) abandoned efforts to recover a robotic probe sent into a damaged reactor at the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear plant, after it became stuck 10 meters in due to a blocked path. The robot, deployed for the first time to measure radiation and assess debris, successfully collected data from 14 of 18 targeted locations before being disconnected. Despite the setback, the mission provided valuable insights into the still-dangerous conditions inside the reactors, which remain too hazardous for human entry and will require decades and $50 billion to decommission.

More than 500 Houthi rebels have been killed since the start of Saudi-led airstrikes in Yemen, according to a Saudi Defense Ministry official, as the coalition has carried out 1,200 strikes aimed at halting rebel advances. Clashes near the Saudi-Yemeni border resulted in the deaths of three Saudi military officers and injuries to two others after Houthi mortar fire targeted a Saudi site. The conflict has caused significant civilian casualties, with Yemeni and international sources reporting hundreds of deaths and injuries, while the country remains in deep humanitarian crisis.

A small bakery in Hong Kong's Tsim Sha Tsui district has sparked a massive craze for its butter cookies, known as "little bear cookies," with people waiting hours in line to buy them for $9 a tin. The demand has led to a black market, with resellers marking up prices by 70% and counterfeit versions appearing, despite the original store's warnings. This phenomenon mirrors global food crazes like cronuts and ramen burgers, which similarly draw long lines but often fade quickly.

The challenge, promoted by chef Mario Batali and others, aims to raise awareness about the difficulties faced by low-income families, especially after recent cuts to food stamp benefits. Organizers hope the effort will foster empathy and inspire solutions to food insecurity.

A Washington University rowing team practice at Creve Coeur Lake near St. Louis turned chaotic when a swarm of invasive Asian carp jumped from the water and attacked the boat, with one fish landing on team member Devin Patel’s legs, causing him to scream for help. Though no one was injured, the incident left the team shaken and the air thick with the fish’s strong odor. The video of the event, captured by iReporter Benjamin Rosenbaum, shows the startling moment the carp breached the surface and swarmed the boat.

Muhammadu Buhari, a former military ruler, won Nigeria's presidential election in a historic shift, defeating incumbent Goodluck Jonathan and ending the ruling party's long hold on power. In his first interview after the victory, Buhari pledged to aggressively combat corruption, dismantle Boko Haram's influence through regional cooperation, and focus on national security and economic reform. His win marks a democratic milestone for Africa's most populous nation, with Buhari set to be sworn in on May 29 amid hopes for a "new Nigeria."

Thousands of civilians fled west from Ramadi, Iraq, across the Euphrates River bridge into Baghdad after ISIS seized eastern Ramadi and surrounding areas, creating a massive humanitarian exodus marked by exhaustion, trauma, and desperation. Fearing a complete collapse of security, local officials like Faleh Essawi warned Baghdad of imminent disaster, as fighting intensified and rescue efforts failed to arrive.

Amina Ali Qassim and her family fled their home in Yemen’s Birim island after a Saudi-led aerial bombardment destroyed their village, escaping in a crowded fishing boat across the dangerous Bab al-Mandab Strait to Djibouti. (CNN) A small piece of comfort for a family broken by tragedy. In July, Sierra Sharry and Lane Smith were about to welcome their baby. Sharry was eight months pregnant. Then Smith fell and hit his head. He was taken to OU Medical Center in Oklahoma City, but he never got better. "July 13, 2014, was the worst day of my life," Sharry wrote on Facebook. "I lost my best friend. The father of my unborn child." Their son Taos was born a few weeks later. When Taos was six months old, Sharry asked the photographer to help make their family feel whole, just for one photo.

(CNN) You probably already have an opinion about Indiana's religious freedom law. You may agree with the many companies that criticize the law, saying it allows businesses to treat gay and lesbian people unfairly by claiming religion as a reason. Or, like Indiana Governor Mike Pence, you might be surprised by the criticism and say the law is similar to one already used at the federal level and in 19 other states. This issue causes division because debates over religious freedom and gay rights are always emotional. It also raises questions about how the law is understood and what people’s true reasons are for supporting it.

Some people who admire Lucille Ball want her statue taken out of a park in her hometown, Celoron, New York. They say the statue looks unattractive and doesn’t properly represent the "I Love Lucy" star. The life-size bronze statue has been compared to singer Conway Twitty, the snake from "Beetlejuice," and actor Steve Buscemi—none of which are flattering. Even the mayor, Scott Schrecengost, has said he doesn’t like the statue. It shows Lucille Ball holding a bottle of the fake drink Vitameatavegamin, which she used in her show. Still, since it was put up in 2009, the statue has drawn tourists to Celoron, her birthplace, and many visitors take photos

(CNN) The last time Muhammadu Buhari became president of Nigeria, he did so through a military coup. This time, he won through a fair election. Here are five reasons why this one of the most closely fought elections in Nigeria’s history is so important. For the first time ever in Nigeria, the opposition party beat the ruling party in a democratic election. Muhammadu Buhari, who is 72 years old, won the presidential election by about two million votes over the current president, Goodluck Jonathan. Nigeria is important because it has the largest economy and the most people in Africa. It is also one of Africa’s top oil producers and sends a large amount of crude oil to the United States.

(CNN) People in Iran were extremely happy, both online and in the streets—so much so that it felt like the country had won a major victory. This excitement came after a major nuclear deal with the United States and other countries. The deal could end years of strict international sanctions and Iran’s isolation from the global community. In Tehran, on Vali Asr Street, one of the city’s main roads, people celebrated just before midnight. Cars honked, men danced in the middle of traffic, and some people showed off U.S. dollar bills. Young people waved flags from their car roofs, played loud music, and shared messages online using the hashtag #IranTalks.

A fourth man, Dilkhayot Kasimov, has been charged in a case involving a plot to help terrorists and possibly join ISIS, according to a new court document from Brooklyn Federal Court. The three other men already arrested—Abdurasul Hasanovich Juraboev, Akhror Saidakhmetov, and Abror Habibov—were charged with helping a foreign terrorist group. They have all said they are not guilty. It is not known whether Kasimov has been arrested yet.

(CNN) The third blood moon in a series of four was the shortest eclipse. But it was still a great sight for people in North America who got up early. The moon fully entered Earth's shadow at 4:58 a.m. Pacific Time (7:58 a.m. Eastern Time) on Saturday. This started a total lunar eclipse that lasted almost five minutes — the shortest one of the century, according to NASA. For several minutes before, during, and after the eclipse, the moon turned a dark orange color. This color gave the moon the name "blood moon."

Istanbul, Turkey (CNN)  
On Tuesday, many people in Turkey were scared and confused. An older woman wearing a white headscarf and carrying shopping bags stood outside a busy subway station, asking, "What's happening? Why can't I get in?" She was one of millions affected by the worst power outage in over ten years. Dozens of cities across Turkey lost electricity for several hours. Millions of people were impacted, including passengers stuck on stopped trains and subways.

(CNN) This Holy Week, let’s remember what the Bible says about fair pay. Isaiah 58:6 says: This is the kind of fast I want: to stop injustice, end workplace abuse, free those who are trapped, and cancel debts. McDonald's decision to raise wages for 90,000 workers is a big win for fast-food cooks and cashiers, and for everyone who supports them. When fast-food workers stand together, they make it harder for successful companies like McDonald's to pay wages so low that workers can't escape poverty.

(CNN) California may soon have lawns that are more brown than green. Governor Jerry Brown announced new water rules for the first time, requiring homes, businesses, and farms to use 25% less water. This rule applies to cities and towns across the state, which is suffering from a severe drought. "We're in a new era," Brown said. "You won’t be able to water your green grass every day like before." The 25% reduction means about 1.5 million acre-feet less water will be used over the next nine months. One acre-foot of water is about 325,000 gallons.

London (CNN) – Britons have little time left to decide who they want to vote for, as polling stations open across the country in an election that could shift the political scene. The campaign has been very short, especially compared to U.S. elections, where candidates spend years preparing. The election might lead to power switching from David Cameron’s Conservative government to the Labour Party, led by Ed Miliband. Or, it could result in a complicated process where leaders try to form deals with smaller parties. But all that will only happen after the polls close late Thursday evening, local time.

(CNN) This time of year, Christians around the world—more than 2 billion people—think about Jesus’ death and resurrection. Because of the deadly attack on Christian college students in Kenya on Thursday, and the continuing danger faced by Christians in other countries, this Holy Week we are asking Christians to also think about how many Christians and others have been crucified, beheaded, stoned, forced into slavery, sexually abused, trafficked, harassed, bombed, or driven from their homes—just because of their faith. These attacks are carried out by religious extremists.

(CNN) Three city employees in Ferguson, Missouri, either resigned or were fired after racist and offensive emails they sent were made public. The emails were found during a U.S. Justice Department investigation into racism in Ferguson’s police and court systems. The messages included hateful remarks about President Barack Obama, First Lady Michelle Obama, Muslims, and other minorities. The Washington Post obtained the emails on Thursday through a public records request. CNN looked at the emails on Friday. The messages were sent between the city’s top court clerk and two police officers, Police Capt. Rick Henke and Sgt.

Two people, including a licensed greyhound trainer, have been arrested in Australia after at least 55 dog bodies were found dumped in the bush in Queensland, according to media reports. The two suspects are from Bundaberg — a 71-year-old man and a 64-year-old woman. Each was charged with illegally having a firearm. The woman, who is a licensed greyhound trainer, was also charged with trying to stop police. Michael Beatty, a spokesperson for RSPCA Queensland, said the investigation is still ongoing. RSPCA Queensland is helping the police with the case.

Two years ago, Mike Premeau and Kathy Danke started a small business called Memories Gourmet Pizza Co. in their Wisconsin town. They sold frozen pizzas, including breakfast and gluten-free ones, in stores across Nichols, which is west of Green Bay. They built a loyal customer base. But this week, their business was at risk because people confused them with Memories Pizza in Walkerton, Indiana. That restaurant made national news when its owners said they would not cater a same-sex wedding. As a result, angry comments appeared on Memories Gourmet Pizza's Facebook page, and people called the business to protest.

(CNN) A complete camel skeleton, believed to have been used by Ottoman soldiers during the 1600s when they were attacking Vienna, was found under a cellar in Austria. The bones were discovered in 2006–2007 by archaeologists from the University of Veterinary Medicine Vienna (Vetmeduni) while they were studying a site where a shopping center was being built in the town of Tulln. At first, the partly dug-up skeleton was thought to be a large horse or cow. But archaeozoologist Alfred Galik said that when they looked at the neck bones, lower jaw, and forearm bones, they knew right away it was a camel.

Andrew Getty, the 47-year-old grandson of J. Paul Getty, died Tuesday afternoon at his home in Los Angeles, his parents, Ann and Gordon Getty, said in a statement. They asked the media and the public to respect their privacy during this hard time. The Los Angeles County coroner's office said Getty's death seems to have been caused by natural reasons or an accident. Some medicine was found at his home, but officials do not know if he was taking it or what his medical history was.

(CNN) We may never fully understand why co-pilot Andreas Lubitz flew Germanwings Flight 9525 into the French Alps on March 24, killing everyone on board. The latest report shows he quickly dropped the plane toward the ground. This is very frightening. As the investigation continues, we will learn more about how much Lubitz hid his mental illness, or how much help he asked for. How did his depression affect his ability to fly? Should he have quit his job? Should his doctors have warned someone? His case brings up big and important questions about people with mental illness and the shame and fear that often come with it.

There was a flu outbreak in Chicago, but it only affected animals, not people. A plan has been suggested to build a tunnel under the sea connecting Denmark and Germany, with roads and train tracks inside. (CNN) He didn’t say his name. But the name "Gertrude" tattooed on his neck gave him away. That’s what Kankakee County, Illinois, Sheriff Tim Bukowski said on Saturday about Kamron Taylor, a 23-year-old man who was convicted of murder and had escaped from jail. He was caught overnight in Chicago. Authorities across Illinois had been searching for Taylor since early Wednesday, when he attacked a correctional officer at the Kankakee County jail, took the officer’s uniform and SUV, and ran away. The last time officials saw Taylor was on surveillance video, just before midnight Friday, in Chicago. "They saw a man who matched the description," Bukowski said.

As his military service comes to an end, Britain's Prince Harry is going to Australia. He is 30 years old and will arrive on Monday for a four-week stay with the Australian armed forces. He will work and live with Australian Army soldiers in regiments in Sydney, Darwin, and Perth. Prince Harry has previously spent time with Australian troops during his 10-year military career, a military spokesman said.

Two Florida prison guards and one former guard trainee have been charged with planning to kill a former inmate who was about to be released. They used to guard prisons, but now they are in jail. The Florida Attorney General's office said the men were involved in a plot to murder the former inmate. An FBI informant, who had joined a branch of the KKK called the Traditional American Knights of the Ku Klux Klan, met the three men. The informant said that 25-year-old Thomas Jordan Driver told him he had fought with the inmate and that he and 47-year-old David Elliot Moran wanted the man dead. This information came from court documents.

Lausanne, Switzerland (CNN) – A group of world powers called the P5+1 reached a basic agreement with Iran on its nuclear program after a series of intense talks in Lausanne on Thursday. It is still unclear if the agreement will fully succeed. The countries have until the end of June to finalize the details and write the full plan. Still, the talks were a major step, especially for the long-stalled relationship between the U.S. and Iran. The negotiations were not flashy, but they showed both the best and the most stressful parts of modern diplomacy.

An improvised bomb exploded near a U.N. vehicle in the northeastern Somali city of Garowe on Monday morning. Six people were killed, including four aid workers from UNICEF. Somalia’s president said the attack was "an attack against the future of our country." This happened shortly after another incident on Sunday, when three African Union soldiers died in an ambush in the Lower Shabelle region of Somalia. The terrorist group Al-Shabaab said it carried out Monday’s attack. The explosion happened around 8 a.m. in Garowe, which is the capital of the Puntland region, according to the United Nations Assistance Mission in Somalia.

(CNN) Prince Harry, 30, arrived in Australia on Monday. He will spend four weeks there serving with the Australian military. Before starting his duties, he visited the Australian War Memorial in Canberra, the capital, and paid his respects at the Tomb of the Unknown Australian Soldier. Many people gathered outside the memorial. Some took photos of him, and one boy held a sign that said, "Red Heads Rule!" because of Harry's hair color. The Australian Defence Forces said he will live and work with soldiers in different army units in Sydney, Darwin, and Perth.

Australia, a key ally of the United States, has agreed to share some of its intelligence with Iran. Australian Foreign Minister Julie Bishop said the agreement is informal and mainly focuses on tracking Australians who travel to Iraq to fight for ISIS. One Australian politician called the move "dancing with the devil." Bishop recently became the first Australian government minister in 12 years to visit Iran, where she met with President Hassan Rouhani. The intelligence deal was announced in an interview Bishop gave to the Australian Broadcasting Corporation while she was in Tehran.

Marseille, France (CNN) – Initial tests on the flight data recorder from the crashed Germanwings Flight 9525 show that co-pilot Andreas Lubitz intentionally made the plane descend faster. The French air accident investigation agency, the BEA, said this. The flight data recorder, also called the "black box," was found on Thursday by recovery teams who had searched for days in the French Alps where the plane crashed on March 24. On Friday, the BEA said its teams started looking at the data right away.

(CNN) A 110-day chase from Antarctic waters to the west African coast ended unexpectedly when the crew of a suspected illegal fishing ship were rescued by conservationists who had been chasing them. The environmental group Sea Shepherd had been tracking the Thunder, which was wanted by Interpol for suspected fraud and fishing crimes, since it was first spotted by the Bob Barker in the Southern Ocean months earlier. The chase ended early Monday in the Gulf of Guinea, off west Africa, when the Bob Barker received a distress call from the Thunder.

Most days, 16-year-old Jason Zobott arrives at Huntley High School, a school in the suburbs of Chicago, around 7:30 a.m., like most high school students. What makes his day different is how he spends the rest of it. Jason is in Huntley High’s blended learning program, which combines online classes with regular classroom teaching. One-third of the school’s 2,700 students are in the program, and the school hopes to have most students enrolled by 2015. Jason, a top student who also takes part in many after-school activities, says he likes learning online because it helps him get his work done. He says he can learn at his own pace.

Garissa, Kenya (CNN) – After a deadly Al-Shabaab attack in Kenya, the Kenyan military carried out airstrikes against the group in Somalia. A military source said these strikes were not revenge for the recent attack at Garissa University College, which killed almost 150 people. The source said the airstrikes are part of a military operation that began in 2011 and has continued ever since. The source did not give their name, as is common for Kenyan military officials speaking to the media.

Pope Francis spoke at the end of Easter Mass and reminded people that the Vatican is a country and that he serves as a moral leader. He expressed sadness over the suffering caused by ongoing wars, especially in Iraq and Syria. He called for an end to violence in those places and urged that help reach people who need it. He also asked the global community not to ignore the serious humanitarian crisis in these countries or the struggles of the many refugees. His message was given in Latin, meaning "to the city (Rome) and to the world."

(CNN) Students and staff at Duke University marched on Wednesday afternoon, shouting, "We are not afraid. We stand together," after a noose was found hanging from a tree on campus. Duke officials are asking anyone who knows anything about the noose—found near a student center at 2 a.m.—to contact campus police. Pictures of the noose spread quickly on social media, causing anger in the community. Hundreds of people gathered at a forum on the steps of Duke Chapel, close to where the noose was found. One speaker said, "You came here because you want to say with me: 'This is not the Duke we will accept. This is not the Duke we want. This is not the Duke we’re here to experience.'"

A U.S. citizen linked to al Qaeda did not plead guilty during his first court hearing on Thursday. He is charged with planning to help terrorists by providing support. Muhanad Mahmoud Al Farekh, 29, was sent back from Pakistan to the U.S. He is accused of trying to fight against U.S. troops overseas. The charges were made public in a court document filed in U.S. District Court in Brooklyn. A CNN counterterrorism expert said this news is good to hear.

Sanaa, Yemen (CNN) – A Saudi border guard was killed in a fight across the border with Yemen on Wednesday night. The Saudi Press Agency (SPA) reported the incident on Thursday. This is the first time Saudi Arabia has publicly confirmed a military death since it started bombing rebels in Yemen.

The fighting happened in the Asir region in southwestern Saudi Arabia. Militants in a mountainous area of Yemen fired on Saudi border troops. In response, the Saudi troops fired back.

The dead guard was identified as Corporal Salman Ali Yahya al-Maliki. Ten other people were injured, but their injuries were not serious.

Dubai (CNN) I feel a little nervous as I go to the Al Marmoum camel race in Dubai. As the only Gulf national on the CNN team, people expect me to know about camel racing, a long-standing tradition here. But even though I tried wearing a kandora, the traditional UAE clothing, my modern way of life makes me feel like a stranger in this world. A friendly farm owner takes us into the majlis, a special meeting area, where camel owners are gathering. The room is large and beautifully decorated, like a theater. The camel owners are sitting on the floor, eating a'aish—a traditional Arabic meal of fish and rice—placed in front of them. The talk is loud and full of energy.

Havana, Cuba (CNN) – Charlie Hill is sitting in a dark bar on a very sunny day in Havana. "Hey man," he says, his voice rough from smoking, nodding as if he knows you’ve been looking for him. But a lot of people have been looking for him for a long time. For 43 years, Cuba has protected him from being charged in the case where he is accused of killing a New Mexico police officer and hijacking an airplane to Havana. Hill is now 65 years old. He decided to talk to CNN after we spent two years trying to find him. He wants to talk about something new: for the first time, he is thinking about leaving Cuba and going back to the United States.

Misao Okawa, who was recognized by Guinness World Records as the world’s oldest person, has died at age 117. She passed away on Wednesday morning in Osaka, Japan, according to Tadahi Uchimura, a local official. She had three children, four grandchildren, and six great grandchildren. Okawa was born on March 5, 1898. Her family owned a kimono shop in Osaka. Satoshi Yoshioka, an employee at the nursing home where she lived since 1997, said she was a calm person who loved to eat. Her favorite foods were sushi and udon noodles. She had eaten a lot of cake on her birthday in March 2018.

Washington (CNN) – When the Missouri National Guard got ready to send troops to Ferguson, Missouri, to help stop riots that happened off and on last year, they used strong military language like "enemy forces" and "adversaries" to describe the protesters. The guard went to help local police, who many community leaders and civil rights groups said used too much force and made an already tense situation worse. Protests in Ferguson happened occasionally from August until the end of the year.

Mogadishu, Somalia (CNN) – On Tuesday, gunmen attacked the Somalia government's education ministry building in the capital. The attack started with a suicide car bomb at the front of the two-story building. At least 12 people were killed and 16 were injured, officials said. The Islamist group Al-Shabaab claimed responsibility. Their spokesman, Abu Musab, said the group carried out the attack. After the bomb, five armed men entered the building and began shooting people inside. The Somali National Security Ministry spokesman, Mohamed Yusuf, confirmed these details.

(CNN) Gregory Margolin is now 87 years old. When he was 16, he joined the Soviet Red Army as a Jewish soldier. He fought against the Nazis in World War II. At that time, his family had to flee. He says he didn’t show he was Jewish, but it didn’t matter because so many people were dying all around him. This year, he found himself in Ukraine, once again in the middle of war. He had been a sniper and later became a military commander. His old uniform still has the medals he earned during the war. His granddaughter, Liora, still listens to his war stories with amazement. She can’t believe he lived through it all.

(CNN) How could over 200 Nigerian schoolgirls just vanish? And why did the Nigerian government and the rest of the world do so little to stop it? It has now been exactly 365 days since the girls were taken from their dorm rooms at a boarding school in Chibok, in northeastern Nigeria. They are still missing. We should all feel ashamed—ashamed that in our world, young girls can be taken and harmed without punishment by violent extremists. And ashamed that after such terrible events, people quickly stop paying attention.

(CNN) Video may have replaced the radio star, but in Norway, it's digital radio that is replacing FM radio. In two years, Norway will be the first country in the world to completely stop using FM radio. That doesn’t mean people will have no radio at all—just that they’ll need to switch to digital radio. In Oslo, officials say many people in this country of 5 million have already made the switch. Right now, only five radio stations are available on FM. On digital radio, there are four times as many—20 stations. Half of Norway’s population already listens to radio through the digital system, said Culture Minister Thorhild Widvey.

Everyone likes a great comeback story — especially one involving a dinosaur. For over 100 years, the Brontosaurus was not considered a separate type of dinosaur and was removed from science books. But a new study says it should be recognized as its own type. In 1879, O.C. Marsh named the Brontosaurus after finding 25 crates of bones at Como Bluff, Wyoming, according to the Yale Peabody Museum of Natural History. It looked similar to, but not as big as, the Apatosaurus, which had been discovered a few years earlier. Marsh gave it the name "Brontosaurus," meaning "thunder lizard."

(CNN) Al Qaeda has offered 20 kilograms of gold—worth about $774,000—to anyone who kills or captures two major Shia Muslim leaders in Yemen. The two men are Houthi leader Abdelmalik Bedrudin Al-Houthi and former Yemeni President Ali Abdullah Saleh. The offer was made by Al Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula (AQAP), which is based in Yemen. AQAP called Al-Houthi and Saleh the "two heads of evil" in a news release and poster shared online. AQAP is one of many groups fighting for control of Yemen.

(CNN) Before landing his gyrocopter on the Capitol lawn on Wednesday, Doug Hughes posted his plans and reasons on a website called thedemocracyclub.org. The 61-year-old Florida postal worker wrote in a post titled "Your Pilot" that the flight was meant to draw attention to corruption in Washington, D.C., and to share solutions to government corruption. He said the flight was not a surprise. Before taking off, he emailed info@barackobama.com to tell the people in charge at the Capitol that he was not a threat. He wanted to show that shooting him down would cause more problems than letting him deliver his messages to Congress.

(CNN) More bad news for Rio de Janeiro came when many dead fish were found in the Rodrigo de Freitas lagoon, just over a year before the city hosts the rowing and canoe events for the 2016 Olympics. On Monday, officials from Rio de Janeiro’s legislative assembly started an investigation into why the fish died, not just in this lagoon but also in other lakes and bays across the state. The investigation will be done with help from the State Environmental Institute (INEA) and the State Secretariat for the Environment.

Anthony Ray Hinton is 58 years old. But in many ways, he is just starting to experience life as most people do. Simple things like using a fork, going out at night, or going to bed without someone watching over him are new to him. This is because he spent almost 30 years on Alabama’s death row. Just one week ago, his murder convictions were overturned, and he left a county jail in Birmingham. "I have to pinch myself to believe I’m free," he told CNN’s Brooke Baldwin. "It will take time, but I’ll get used to it." For 30 years, he mostly lived in a small 5-by-7-foot cell.

(CNN) After the UK election debate featuring seven party leaders—David Cameron (Conservatives), Ed Miliband (Labour), Nick Clegg (Liberal Democrats), Nigel Farage (UK Independence Party), Natalie Bennett (Green Party), Nicola Sturgeon (Scottish National Party), and Leanne Wood (Plaid Cymru, Welsh Nationalists)—there was no clear winner. According to a Comres poll for ITV, which hosted the debate, Cameron, Miliband, and Farage each got 21% support, while Sturgeon got 20%. An ICM poll for The Guardian gave Miliband 25%, Cameron 24%, Farage 19%, and Sturgeon 17%.

(CNN) Facebook might soon have to add "Just got served divorce papers" as a relationship status, after a New York judge ruled that sending divorce papers through the social media site is a valid way to serve a man in Brooklyn. Ellanora Arthur Baidoo has been trying to divorce her husband, Victor Sena Blood-Dzraku, for several years, her lawyer Andrew Spinnell said. But they have not been able to find him to serve the papers. Baidoo has called him before, and he told her he doesn’t have a fixed address or a job, according to court documents.

(CNN) This sounds like a scene from a sci-fi movie. Someone has a terrible accident and ends up in the hospital, brain dead and on life support. Doctors talk to the family about donating organs, but instead of saving up to eight lives, the family is asked to donate the whole body to save just one person—maybe someone who is paralyzed but has a sharp mind trapped in a broken body. Even though this idea seems wild, Italian doctor Dr. Sergio Canavero says we are getting close to making it real. He calls this plan HEAVEN, which stands for Head Anastomosis Venture. Anastomosis means joining two parts together through surgery.

(CNN) Anthony Stokes was supposed to have a happy ending. Instead, police say, he died on Tuesday after carjacking someone, breaking into a house, shooting at an older woman, leading police on a high-speed chase, and crashing into a pole. In 2013, his family said an Atlanta hospital turned him down for a heart transplant because he had a history of not following medical advice, according to a letter from the hospital. At the time, Mark Bell was speaking for the Stokes family.

The sun had not yet risen at Garissa University College. Most students were still asleep in their beds. A few had gotten up to go to early morning Christian prayers. Then, at about 5:30 a.m. on Thursday (10:30 p.m. Wednesday in New York), an explosion and gunshots happened at the school’s front gates. The attackers kept shooting as they moved through the campus. The Red Cross said they stopped at a dormitory for girls. At one point, they broke into a room where Christians were praying and took some people hostage, said lecturer Joel Ayora.

(CNN) A white casket was at the front of New Shiloh Baptist Church in West Baltimore while a gospel choir sang for a large crowd. The crowd came to honor Freddie Gray, a 25-year-old man who died 15 days earlier while in police custody. He was arrested on a weapons charge. He died from a serious spinal cord injury. His death caused strong anger toward the Baltimore Police Department. Gray’s death is part of a recent series of well-known cases where African-Americans died during encounters with police. Many people are asking what really happened to Gray. His funeral was attended by civil rights leaders, politicians, and family members of others who died in police custody.

I’ve worked as a chef since I was 14, but I didn’t start fighting for food justice until later. In 2007, my wife’s mentee—a young girl—was caught looking through trash for food. That moment changed me. I started Food Policy Action and got involved in food issues like hunger and factory farming. I wasn’t alone. A big influence was "The Meatrix," a 2003 video parody of "The Matrix" made by the GRACE Communications Foundation. It clearly showed the dangers of factory farming to health and the environment.

(CNN) Dan Swangard knows what death looks like. As a doctor, he has seen patients die in hospitals, on morphine, feeling scared and anxious. He has seen people suffer for weeks or months, while family members watch helplessly. Recently, though, his thoughts about dying have become personal. In 2013, he was diagnosed with a rare type of cancer that has spread. To treat it, doctors removed parts of his pancreas and liver, as well as his entire spleen and gallbladder. The surgery worked, but Swangard, who is 48, knows there is a high chance the cancer will come back.

(CNN) Saudi special forces helped Yemeni fighters attack Houthis and their allies in Aden, a Saudi source told CNN. The special forces were on the ground but not fighting. They were helping by coordinating and directing the fight against Houthi forces and fighters loyal to former Yemeni President Ali Abdullah Saleh. They also helped drop weapons and communication equipment by parachute. Meanwhile, the Houthis pulled back from the presidential palace and other important areas in Aden after strong Saudi airstrikes. This retreat came after the Houthis had taken control of the presidential palace the day before.

A mother from Detroit was arrested last month after police found the bodies of two of her children in a freezer. She appeared in court this week and was charged with murder and torture. Wayne County Prosecutor Kym Worthy said the mother, Mitchelle Angela Blair, is accused of killing her 13-year-old daughter, Stoni Ann Blair, and her 9-year-old son, Stephen Gage Berry. The bodies were discovered on March 24 by a bailiff during a court-ordered eviction. The bodies were wrapped in plastic and found inside the freezer. The Wayne County medical examiner said Stoni died from multiple blunt force injuries. Stephen died from multiple blunt force injuries and burns.

Miami (CNN) – Wladimir Klitschko, the world heavyweight boxing champion, has an important fight coming up on April 25 against American boxer Bryant Jennings in New York. But he is still deeply affected by the ongoing struggle for democracy in his home country, Ukraine. Speaking from his training base in Miami, Klitschko said the war between Ukraine and Russia has shocked and upset him. He said Ukraine did not start the conflict and was not the one who attacked Russia. Instead, he said Russia is the one causing the problems.

"It's showtime!" Michael Keaton returned as host of "Saturday Night Live" for the third time this weekend. He made a small nod to his famous roles in "Beetlejuice" and "Batman" during his opening monologue. He joked that a lot has changed since he first hosted the show in 1982, saying he now has a 31-year-old son and a 28-year-old girlfriend. Fans hoping to see him fully reprise his most famous characters were not satisfied. Cast members Taran Killam and Bobby Moynihan even sang a song asking him to play Batman and Beetlejuice with them. But Keaton only gave them a few short jokes in return.

(CNN) About a month ago, Kamron Taylor was found guilty of murder in an Illinois court. Early Wednesday morning, he was in an Illinois jail, hiding in his cell, waiting to attack. When he did, he attacked a jail guard who was on duty, according to Kankakee County Sheriff Timothy Bukowski. Taylor hit the guard, put on the guard’s uniform and took his keys. He then walked out of the jail and got into the guard’s brown 2012 Chevrolet Equinox SUV. The 23-year-old, who was supposed to be sentenced in May, is now missing. The SUV was found around 8:30 a.m. (9:30 a.m.

A New York City detective has been suspended after being accused of stealing $3,000 during a raid on illegal cigarettes. Police spokesman Stephen Davis said the incident happened last Friday at the Yemen Deli and Grocery store in Brooklyn. Surveillance video from CNN's affiliate News 12 Brooklyn shows Detective Ian Cyrus putting cash into a bag before leaving the store. The detectives had arrested two store employees for selling loose cigarettes. The store’s manager, Ali Abdullah, noticed the money was missing from a box. He thought one of his employees had taken it. But when he checked the video, he was shocked by what he saw.

London (CNN) – The Hatton Garden heist will likely be remembered as one of the most daring crimes ever. Thieves used heavy cutting tools and rappelling gear to break into the vault of a well-known 60-year-old safe deposit company in central London over the holiday weekend. They may have had as long as four days to search through an unknown number of safe deposit boxes. They are believed to have stolen hundreds of thousands of pounds worth of gems and cash. One former police official thinks they might have taken as much as 200 million pounds, or about $300 million.

(CNN) On April 27, South Africa will mark the anniversary of its first post-apartheid elections in 1994. At the same time, the country is dealing with another wave of violent attacks on African migrants. People are angry about this violence, and many are speaking out on social media using the hashtag "#WeAreAfrica" to show that they stand together against such attacks. These repeated attacks on migrants and their property suggest that South Africa’s dream of a united, multi-racial society may not be coming true. That dream was about a country where people of all races and backgrounds could live with dignity.

In 1989, Ayatollah Khomeini said he was "drinking poison" when he agreed to stop the war with Iraq. The war had helped shape his government, the Islamic Republic, which he had created just a year before Saddam Hussein attacked Iran. Khomeini united his supporters and others against the enemy and kept the war going for eight years, even though Saddam wanted to stop. This helped keep his government strong. By the time the war ended, the economy was broken, and many of his loyal fighters were gone.

(CNN) The idea of sustainable development is that uncontrolled capitalism is too strong and harmful to itself. The global economy is growing very fast—doubling every generation. But Earth has limited resources, and a billion more people are added every 15 years. This rapid growth is now damaging the natural world and the social systems that help people live well. Sustainable development provides a way to solve this worsening problem. In reality, uncontrolled capitalism is based on greed.

The United States has benefited greatly from being a space-faring nation. Space access has helped protect national security, support the military, and boost the economy. To handle today’s and future conflicts, fight terrorism, and deal with growing global threats, the U.S. military depends on space-based systems like intelligence gathering, GPS, and communication satellites. However, as threats around the world grow and the need for reliable space access becomes more urgent, the U.S. faces a serious problem: it still depends too much on Russian technology to carry out its national security duties.

On the day before the first anniversary of when almost 300 schoolgirls were taken by Boko Haram in Nigeria, Malala Yousafzai sent an open letter to them. She wrote, "Like you, I was attacked by militants who didn’t want girls to go to school." Malala, a 17-year-old Nobel Peace Prize winner, survived a Taliban attack in Pakistan because she had spoken out about the need for girls to stay in school. In her letter, she asks the Nigerian government and the world to do more to bring the girls home. Nigeria recently had an election.

Johannesburg, South Africa – On Tuesday evening, South African soldiers were sent in to help stop violent attacks against immigrants. Their first stop was Jeppestown, a suburb of Johannesburg, where such violence started on Friday. Police searched a hostel in Jeppestown on Tuesday, while soldiers guarded the area. Earlier, Defense Minister Nosiviwe Mapisa-Nqakula said the government would send an unknown number of troops to places where police are too few to stop deadly attacks on immigrants. She said this move is not a criticism of the police.

Eight Iranian border guards were killed in fighting with armed militants near the border with Pakistan, according to Iranian state media. Three of the militants were killed by Iranian forces on Monday in the southeastern town of Negur, as reported by the state news agency IRNA. The agency said that Ali Asghar Mirshekari, the deputy governor of Iran's Sistan-Baluchestan province, stated the militants had entered Iran from Pakistan. Iranian officials have asked Pakistani authorities to find and arrest the remaining attackers.

(CNN) If you like visiting many islands, you should know that Providenciales in the Turks and Caicos has been named the best island in the world by TripAdvisor. It moved up one spot from last year’s second place to take the top spot, pushing Ambergris Caye in Belize out of first. Ambergris Caye had been number one for two years straight, but this year it fell out of the top 10. TripAdvisor spokeswoman Julie Cassetina said it’s hard to explain why the rankings change each year, since they are based on traveler feedback.

The "Star Wars" story is growing. At the Star Wars Celebration fan event in Anaheim, California, on Sunday, details about the 2016 movie "Star Wars: Rogue One" were shared. Director Gareth Edwards, who made "Godzilla," showed a short preview of the film and gave more information about the movie. It is part of the "Star Wars" anthology series (what Disney calls a "spinoff"). Felicity Jones stars in the film. The story takes place between "Episode III: Revenge of the Sith" and "Episode IV: A New Hope" (the first "Star Wars" movie from 1977). A group of rebels carries out a secret mission to steal the plans for the Death Star. Jones plays a rebel soldier.

Tehran, Iran (CNN)  
A Persian saying goes: "A good year is decided by its spring." For many Iranians, the recent decision by Tehran and six world powers—the U.S., UK, France, Germany, Russia, and China—to keep negotiating on Iran’s nuclear program under a "joint comprehensive plan of action" is a sign that this year’s Norouz, the Persian New Year that began on March 21, will be a very good one. While some strict hardliners may now argue or complain that the first agreement isn’t exactly what they wanted, most people see it as strong progress—and that’s what they care about.

Ferguson, Missouri (CNN) – At 11:45 p.m. ET, two African-Americans, Ella Jones and Wesley Bell, won seats on the Ferguson City Council. This means three of the six council members are now Black. Earlier, at 6:52 p.m. ET, the city began its municipal election voting at 6 a.m. The weather was bad, with dark skies and flash flood warnings on the radio. Normally, few people vote in Ferguson’s city elections. But this time was different. It was the first election since white police officer Darren Wilson shot and killed unarmed Black teenager Michael Brown in August. Since then, the city has been under national attention.

One Israeli man was killed and another was hurt in an incident police believe was a terror attack on Wednesday night near Hebrew University in Jerusalem. A 37-year-old Arab man from East Jerusalem drove into two people waiting at a bus stop in the French Hill area. The victim who died was identified as Shalom Yohai Cherki, 26. A 20-year-old woman is still in serious condition. The driver has been arrested and is being investigated by Israel's General Security Services.

An art collection put together by the late actress Lauren Bacall, a famous Hollywood star, is now for sale. The collection includes pieces by some of the most famous artists of the 1900s. It was sold in New York on March 31, after being shown in Hong Kong, Paris, London, and Los Angeles. Bacall died in August 2014 at age 89. She became famous worldwide in 1944 with her first movie, "To Have And Have Not," and met her future husband, Humphrey Bogart, at that time. In 2015, at the Golden Globes, George Clooney honored Bacall in his award speech.

Kiev, Ukraine (CNN) – People in Kiev are wondering who is killing people who supported Ukraine’s former president, Viktor Yanukovych. This concern isn’t new, but it has become more urgent this week after two high-profile killings in the capital. One was a former member of parliament linked to Yanukovych. The other was a Ukrainian journalist who supported Russia. Oleg Kalashnikov, the former lawmaker, was shot and killed just after 7 p.m. on Wednesday at the entrance to his apartment building.

(CNN) Same-sex civil unions will soon be recognized in Chile. President Michelle Bachelet signed a new law on Monday that allows these unions, making Chile one of several South American countries to do so. Bachelet said this is a real step toward ending the difference between gay and straight couples. The law will start in six months. It will give legal rights to couples living together, whether they are two men, two women, or a man and a woman. The government says about 2 million people will be able to benefit from this change.

The next time you fly to visit Grandma in Florida, or take the kids to see the talking mouse or go to South Beach for sun and fun, sit by the window and look down as you land. You’ll see a huge, wet, swampy area below. This is the Everglades — a place that shows how people have made big mistakes and how hard it is to fix them. As you fly into Miami or Orlando, it may look like a messy, dangerous swamp full of things that can hurt you — snakes, scorpions, rats, roaches, alligators, and mosquitoes. One scientist once caught 365,000 biting bugs in just one trap in one night.

(CNN) Masked men flooded into Yarmouk, a Palestinian refugee camp near Damascus that has been under siege and bombed by Syrian forces for over two years. In early April, residents woke up to find ISIS fighters had taken control of the camp after defeating several local militia groups. One resident, who did not want to be named, told CNN, "They killed them in the streets. They caught three people and killed them right in front of others. The Islamic State now controls almost all of the camp."

(CNN) China has used the "Great Firewall" for years to block its people from reading critical articles from Western news sites or seeing other content the government doesn’t like. But a new study released on Friday says this isn’t enough anymore. Chinese cybercensors have created a new tool called the "Great Cannon" and have used it to attack servers outside China, including in the United States. The study’s authors say the Great Cannon works openly and can be seen. They also believe that attacking servers in another country so clearly will likely upset other nations, but Beijing may have expected that.

The investigation into the crash of Germanwings Flight 9525 has not found any proof of why co-pilot Andreas Lubitz did what he did. But a spokesman for the prosecutor's office in Dusseldorf, Germany, said Lubitz had shown signs of suicidal thoughts before he started his career as a pilot. Investigators have not found any notes, messages, or talks where Lubitz explained his actions or admitted to any plans. However, medical records show that Lubitz was suicidal at one time and had received therapy. This happened before he ever got his pilot's license, the spokesman said.

(CNN) The head of Yemen's Houthi rebels said on Sunday that his fighters would not leave major cities or government buildings. He told reporters in a TV speech, "Anyone who thinks we will give up is just dreaming." His statement came after more than three weeks of airstrikes by a Saudi-led coalition. The goal of the bombings was to stop the Houthis, who took control of the capital, Sanaa, in January and forced President Abdu Rabu Mansour Hadi to flee.

On April 19, 1995, Timothy McVeigh set off a large truck bomb in front of the Murrah Federal Building in Oklahoma City. The explosion killed 168 people, including men, women, and children, and injured many others. It remains the worst case of domestic terrorism in U.S. history. The event shocked the nation and received widespread media attention. Reports described it as an "attack on the heartland" and said it marked the end of America's "lost innocence." The bombing was surprising because it was not just the size of the tragedy that stood out, but also because it showed that American citizens could attack their own government with a level of violence that had never been seen before.

(CNN) If you really cared about something, would you protest? Make a sign? Join a march? How long would you keep doing it if no one listened or acted? A year ago, more than 200 Nigerian schoolgirls were taken by Boko Haram fighters. Millions of people worldwide joined a social media campaign to demand their safe return. Charles Alasholuyi was one of them — along with celebrities and world leaders — using the hashtag #BringBackOurGirls. It became one of the most used Twitter hashtags of 2014, appearing in over four million tweets. But as weeks turned into months, the girls still hadn’t been found. The attention on the campaign slowly disappeared.

(CNN) Barney Frank, who has spent a long time in politics, recently spoke in Chicago to a full crowd at the Center on Halsted. He shared stories from his 45 years in public service. Frank was the first member of Congress to marry someone of the same sex while still in office. He also spoke strongly against politicians who hide their sexuality and vote against LGBT rights. When someone in the audience asked about a California ballot measure that would allow killing gay people, Frank said he didn’t know about the proposal. He told the young man not to worry about “crazy people.”

A violent attack on Garissa University College in Kenya has killed almost 150 people, including students, and injured many others. The attack happened early Thursday morning during prayers. Armed men opened fire randomly, took people hostage, and were later killed by security forces. The U.S. Embassy in Nairobi said Al-Shabaab, a militant group, claimed responsibility. This attack follows a similar incident months earlier, when Al-Shabaab killed non-Muslim workers at a quarry in Kenya. The group has carried out many attacks in the region and has also recruited some Americans, especially from the Somali-American community in Minnesota.

A university in South Africa is celebrating the removal of a statue of Cecil Rhodes, a British colonial figure, after weeks of protests. Students from the University of Cape Town used social media to call for the statue to be taken down, saying Rhodes' history is linked to racism. They started a campaign using the hashtag #RhodesMustFall last month. Four weeks later, the hashtag is now #RhodesHasFallen. The university said on Wednesday that a heritage group gave permission to remove the statue from campus. The university added that the removal is to keep the statue safe while decisions are made about what to do with it next.

(CNN) Syria is a place of extreme suffering that is getting worse. If an opposition group is correct, the number of people killed there has doubled in one year. Since the civil war began, 310,000 people have died, according to the Syrian Observatory for Human Rights (SOHR), which reported this on Thursday. A year earlier, SOHR had counted 162,402 deaths. The year before that, the United Nations said about 70,000 people had been killed. More than half of all Syrians are now in desperate need of help, the UN says, because violence has destroyed their lives. Food aid is being reduced because there are not enough donations.

(Ailina Tsarnaeva entered Manhattan Criminal Court quietly and appeared shy. But prosecutors say she was not afraid to threaten a woman she saw as a rival. In a phone call this summer, according to a criminal complaint, she told the woman, "Leave my man alone. Stop looking for him. I know people who can put a bomb where you live." Because of who she is—the sister of Dzhokhar and Tamerlan Tsarnaev—prosecutors took the threat seriously and charged her with aggravated harassment. She denies the charge. Last December, after leaving court, she and her lawyer refused to talk about the case.)

A door painted with graffiti by British artist Banksy was taken by police in Gaza on Thursday after a dispute over its sale, a Gaza police official told CNN. The door’s owner, Rabea Darduna, said he didn’t know its value and sold it for just $175. He later filed a complaint with a Gaza court. The iron door is now being held by the Khan Younis police in southern Gaza. A court hearing will happen at a later date, but the date has not been set. Darduna said his home in Gaza was destroyed during last summer’s war, and he felt he had nothing left—only a doorway and a door.

(CNN) Fighting against the Houthi rebels in Yemen went on Tuesday. The Saudi-led coalition said it is gaining more control, but many people are fleeing the violence, and the death toll is rising — dozens of those killed are civilians. Five days after their first airstrikes, the coalition has destroyed most of the Houthis' and former President Ali Abdullah Saleh's supporters' air defense systems. Almost all air bases and runways are now unusable, according to a Saudi source. Saudi Arabia's navy now controls all Yemeni ports. Only non-military medical supplies are allowed through the blockade, and they are closely monitored.

Holland's manager Guus Hiddink criticized his own fans for booing Andres Iniesta during Holland's 2-0 win over Spain on Tuesday night. He called the fans' behavior a "disgrace." Spain's coach Vicente del Bosque used a practice team, and Iniesta came on in the 76th minute. He was met with loud boos from the home crowd at the Amsterdam Arena. Stefan de Vrij and Davy Klaassen scored in the first half to give Holland the win. But Hiddink was upset that Iniesta was treated that way. Iniesta played for Spain, which lost 2-0 to Holland.

Scotland will find out on May 21 whether their September 2016 Euro 2016 match against Georgia will be played without fans. UEFA has started disciplinary action against the Georgian Football Federation (GFF) because fans ran onto the field twice during Georgia’s 2-0 loss to Germany in Tbilisi on Sunday. UEFA will also investigate reports that home fans set off fireworks, and look into safety problems at the Boris Paichadze Stadium, including blocked stairs, locked gates, and staff not doing body searches. A fan ran onto the pitch during the game in Tbilisi.

Football agents were unsure on Wednesday while waiting for new rules. Starting April 1, anyone can become a football agent by paying £500 for a one-year registration. After that, the Football Association (FA) will charge £250 each year to keep the license. Agents who were already licensed do not have to follow the new rules. The FA was supposed to put a link on its website so agents could register, but as of 1pm, that link was still not there. Mel Stein says the new rules could cause chaos. The changes came after FIFA stopped overseeing football agents.

Maksims Uvarenko, a Latvian goalkeeper for CSKA Sofia, hasn't been paid for three months and had to ask his parents to send him money for rent. He joined the Bulgarian club on an 18-month contract in January. Even though he's facing money problems, he says he's impressed by the fans and their strong support. Uvarenko told local media that not getting paid is the biggest problem he's had at CSKA. He still hasn't received any salary after three months with the club.
